scenarios.intro: After yesterday's community meeting Patryk said he wants to discharge himself. You're on duty. Patryk stands in the doorway with a half-packed bag.

nodes.client: I'm packing. I've had enough of this place. Five weeks and I feel fine, I don't need another seven. I'm just wasting my time here.

options.text: Five weeks isn't enough. If you leave now, you'll go back to using.
options.feedback: A gloomy prediction provokes an 'I'll prove you wrong' reaction.

options.text: What happened that made you decide to pack today?
options.feedback: The open question looks for the trigger – often an emotion rather than a considered choice.

options.text: You feel well enough that the next weeks seem like a waste of time.
options.feedback: The reflection accepts his perspective without a fight – he doesn't need to defend it.

options.text: Have you talked to your key therapist yet?
options.feedback: A procedural question passes him on instead of listening to him.

nodes.client: Yesterday at community I got some harsh feedback. Everyone was on at me. And my girlfriend keeps texting that she misses me and I should come back.

options.text: Feedback is part of therapy. You need to take it, not run away.
options.feedback: Lecturing him while he's hurt reinforces the sense that everyone's against him.

options.text: Good that you came to talk instead of just walking out.
options.feedback: Affirming his choice to talk strengthens the relationship, though it doesn't deepen the topic yet.

options.text: Yesterday's meeting really hurt, and missing her makes leaving seem like the easiest option right now.
options.feedback: The reflection connects two sources of strain and shows the decision is driven by feelings.

nodes.client: Everyone says that. I'm not like the rest of them here. I'll sort myself out.

options.text: You believe you can do it on your own.
options.feedback: The simple reflection doesn't challenge his self-belief – resistance eases.

options.text: It matters to you that nobody lumps you in with everyone else.
options.feedback: The reflection meets his need to be seen as an individual.

options.text: You know, everyone who ends up here says at first that they're not like the rest and will sort themselves out.
options.feedback: An ironic generalisation shames him and escalates the conflict.

nodes.client: Yeah. But actually… it's the first time in two years I've been clean this long. Mum came on Sunday and cried with happiness.

options.text: Then all the more reason not to waste it. You're staying.
options.feedback: Deciding for him takes away the autonomy he was just starting to use.

options.text: What do those five weeks mean to you?
options.feedback: The open question invites him to name the value of his progress himself.

options.text: That's an important change – for you and for your mum.
options.feedback: The reflection reinforces his change talk.

nodes.client: I don't know. It's hard here, but outside… Last time I tried on my own, I lasted a week.

options.text: What went wrong when you tried on your own?
options.feedback: An open question about his experience lets him draw his own conclusions.

options.text: Part of you wants to get away from what's hard, and another part remembers how the last attempt ended.
options.feedback: A double-sided reflection shows the ambivalence and lets him weigh it himself.

options.text: Exactly, that's why you need to finish treatment. Otherwise you'll let your mum and the whole family down again.
options.feedback: Invoking guilt about his family is moralising that provokes rebellion.

options.text: Do you have somewhere to live after you leave?
options.feedback: A practical question, but right now it shifts the talk to the logistics of leaving.

nodes.client: Sure, everyone knows better. Give me the self-discharge form.

options.text: It's your decision and nobody will keep you here by force. I appreciate that you're talking before signing.
options.feedback: Emphasising autonomy and valuing the conversation disarms resistance.

options.text: You're sick of everyone knowing better than you.
options.feedback: The reflection acknowledges his frustration and stops escalation.

options.text: Go ahead. Just don't count on being readmitted later.
options.feedback: The threat closes the door to returning – particularly harmful in addiction treatment.

nodes.client: That I can do it. That I'm not doomed. I'd like to go back to uni, to mechatronics. And for my girlfriend to see me sober.

options.text: I can tell you what has helped others after a tough community meeting, if you like.
options.feedback: Others' experience shared with permission is support, not an order.

options.text: What would help you get through the next difficult days here?
options.feedback: The open question directs him to his own coping strategies.

options.text: Then stay and stop thinking about your girlfriend, she's a distraction.
options.feedback: Dismissing a relationship that matters to him undermines his motivation.

nodes.client: Maybe I'm not ready. But I can't take another community meeting here.

options.text: The problem isn't the therapy itself, it's how you feel at the community meetings.
options.feedback: The reflection narrows the problem to something specific that can be addressed.

options.text: If you can't handle community, you won't handle the outside.
options.feedback: Undermining his capacity at a weak moment pushes him out the door.

options.text: What would make the community meetings bearable?
options.feedback: The open question looks for a solution instead of escape.

nodes.client: Maybe I'll talk to my therapist about that feedback. And ask my girlfriend to come on visiting weekend.

options.text: And apologise to the group for how you reacted yesterday.
options.feedback: An extra demand brings back the sense of judgement and may undo his plan.

options.text: Let me sum up: community hurt, you miss her, but these five weeks have shown you that you can. You want to go back to uni, and for now – talk to your therapist and invite your girlfriend.
options.feedback: The summary links his feelings, values and plan – the decision becomes his.

options.text: You're looking for a solution instead of running. That takes strength.
options.feedback: The affirmation strengthens his self-efficacy.

nodes.client: I don't know. Maybe I'll stay until the weekend and see.

options.text: You don't do therapy 'until the weekend'. Either seriously or not at all.
options.feedback: An all-or-nothing stance rejects his small step and pushes him to leave.

options.text: On one hand community is hard, on the other you don't want a repeat of the last attempt. And you're thinking of staying at least until the weekend.
options.feedback: The summary strengthens his small decision to stay.

options.text: What would need to happen by the weekend for you to want to stay longer?
options.feedback: The open question builds on his statement without undermining it.

nodes.client: OK, I'll unpack. I'll talk to my therapist tomorrow. I'm not promising to stay till the end, but I won't leave today.

options.text: So you're staying for the full twelve weeks?
options.feedback: Demanding a full commitment right away undermines his small, real step.

options.text: What will you do if the thought of leaving comes back tonight?
options.feedback: A plan for the difficult moment reduces the risk of leaving on impulse.

options.text: That's a mature decision – made despite difficult feelings.
options.feedback: Affirming a decision made in crisis strengthens his self-belief.

nodes.client: Thanks. Yesterday I was sure I wouldn't be here today.

ending.title: Crisis weathered
ending.text: Patryk decided to stay himself, based on his own goals and progress. The decision starts with one day – and that's enough for now.

nodes.client: We'll see. I'm staying for now.

ending.title: Staying, for now
ending.text: Patryk stayed, but the end of the conversation brought back the pressure. The risk of discharge at the next hard moment remains high.

nodes.client: Give me the form. I'm out.

ending.title: Self-discharge
ending.text: Confrontation confirmed Patryk's feeling that everyone's against him. After discharge it's worth leaving the door open for return and contact.

scenarios.title: Kuba – first street outreach contact

persona.name: Jakub
persona.description: A young adult who spends evenings with a group in the park by the skatepark. Drinks alcohol, uses mephedrone at weekends. Dropped out of school, not working; his father misuses alcohol at home.

scenarios.intro: Evening, a park on a housing estate. As an outreach worker from a foundation you approach a group of young people on the benches. Kuba seems to be the informal leader and speaks first.

nodes.client: And who are you? Police? Social services? We're just sitting here.

options.text: How old are you?
options.feedback: Asking his age sounds like an ID check and makes him wary.

options.text: Relax. But you know drinking in the park is illegal, right?
options.feedback: Starting with the law puts the outreach worker in a policing role – contact closes.

options.text: You don't know what to expect from me.
options.feedback: Reflecting his distrust shows we understand it – the first step towards trust.

options.text: I'm an outreach worker from a foundation, not the police. What do you usually do here in the evenings?
options.feedback: A transparent introduction and an open question build contact on equal terms.

nodes.client: Oh. Well, we sit, chat, sometimes have a drink, at weekends something stronger. Nobody's waiting for me at home anyway.

options.text: This place and this crew are a bit like home for you.
options.feedback: The complex reflection sees the group's role and his loneliness – Kuba feels understood.

options.text: Thanks for even talking to a stranger. That's not a given.
options.feedback: Affirming his openness strengthens contact, though it misses what's important in his words.

options.text: Be careful with the stronger stuff. Mephedrone is nasty, better not to take it at all.
options.feedback: An unsolicited warning at first contact turns the worker into another adult with a sermon.

nodes.client: So what? Everyone drinks. Get lost, we don't need sermons.

options.text: You've had enough of sermons.
options.feedback: A short reflection accepts his anger without defending.

options.text: I can go, but when a patrol comes by and sees the alcohol, then you'll really be in trouble.
options.feedback: Threatening them with the police destroys the trust street outreach depends on.

options.text: I guess a lot of adults come here just to move you on or lecture you.
options.feedback: The reflection names their experience with adults and sets itself apart from it.

nodes.client: Yeah. At least someone knows me here. But last weekend Bartek went under on meph, he couldn't breathe. I got scared.

options.text: See? You need to stop using before one of you ends up in hospital.
options.feedback: 'See?' uses his fear to lecture him – Kuba will back off.

options.text: What did you do then?
options.feedback: The open question lets him tell a difficult story and reveals how he reacted.

options.text: You were really scared for him.
options.feedback: Reflecting feelings strengthens his concern – a source of motivation for change.

nodes.client: It's going OK. Sometimes better, sometimes worse. No job, I quit school. But I'm not complaining.

options.text: At your age you should be studying or working, not sitting in the park with a beer every evening.
options.feedback: Moralising confirms his picture of adults as people who only judge.

options.text: What does 'worse' look like?
options.feedback: The open question uses his own words and invites honesty.

options.text: Are you looking for work?
options.feedback: The closed question implies an expectation and closes the topic.

options.text: You say you're not complaining, but there's a lot in what you're telling me that seems to bother you.
options.feedback: The reflection gently brings out what's beneath the surface, without pushing.

nodes.client: Seriously? You're not my dad. Go and talk to someone else.

options.text: You don't want a stranger telling you what to do.
options.feedback: The reflection respects his boundary and stops escalation.

options.text: I can go, but if one of you overdoses, don't say nobody warned you.
options.feedback: Threatening his friends' deaths closes contact for a long time.

options.text: Fair enough, it's not for me to judge. Your life, your decisions. I can just leave a leaflet, in case.
options.feedback: Agreeing and emphasising autonomy leaves the door open for future contact.

nodes.client: We called an ambulance, even though we were scared the cops would come. Luckily he made it. Since then I don't really feel like using as much.

options.text: I can tell you what's useful to know in situations like that, to keep things safer. Want to hear?
options.feedback: Harm-reduction information offered with permission is respectful and useful.

options.text: What makes you feel like it less?
options.feedback: The open question develops his change talk.

options.text: Then cut ties with this crew, because next time it could be you.
options.feedback: Ordering him to cut off his only support is unrealistic and provokes resistance.

nodes.client: OK, maybe not everything's great. But what am I supposed to do, sit at home with my dad who's always drunk?

options.text: If you could have something other than the park and home – what would it be?
options.feedback: The question opens space for hopes and alternatives.

options.text: The park is your escape from a home that's even worse.
options.feedback: The reflection names the real context of his choices, without judging.

options.text: That's no excuse. Everyone's responsible for themselves.
options.feedback: Dismissing his hard situation as an excuse breaks contact.

nodes.client: Because I saw how it could end. And actually I'd like to do something, maybe get a forklift licence. A mate did that and he's working.

options.text: For that you need to finish school first. Sign up for adult education.
options.feedback: Setting extra conditions drains the energy from his own idea.

options.text: You acted quickly when Bartek needed help. And you're thinking about the future – that counts.
options.feedback: Affirming his responsible reaction strengthens his self-worth.

options.text: Pulling it together: the crew matters to you, but what happened to Bartek scared you and you feel like using less. And you're thinking about a forklift course.
options.feedback: The summary links his experience and idea – he hears his own direction.

nodes.client: Dunno, mate. I haven't got a plan.

options.text: Without a plan you'll end up like your dad.
options.feedback: Comparing him to his father hurts and destroys trust.

options.text: Home is hard, the park is an escape, and at the same time something about it all bothers you. Not having a plan is an honest answer too.
options.feedback: A summary without pressure accepts where he is and leaves room.

options.text: If things were even a little better in a month, what would that be?
options.feedback: Asking about a small goal lowers the threshold for change.

nodes.client: Will you come by on Thursday? Maybe you could find out about that forklift course. And you can leave those leaflets, the guys will read them too.

options.text: I'll come, but will you promise not to use anything before Thursday?
options.feedback: Making help conditional on abstinence contradicts the low-threshold principle.

options.text: Sure. What else should I find out before Thursday?
options.feedback: The question leaves it to him to decide what he needs.

options.text: I'll come. Great that you're asking yourself – it's your idea, I'm happy to help.
options.feedback: Affirming his initiative and keeping your word are the basis of an outreach relationship.

nodes.client: Right, see you Thursday. Guys, this one's OK.

ending.title: Trust built
ending.text: The first contact ended with a follow-up meeting and an invitation into the group. In street outreach that's a huge success.

nodes.client: Well… we'll see. Maybe I'll be here.

ending.title: Contact on the edge
ending.text: Kuba was open, but conditions and orders weakened trust. Another contact is possible but uncertain.

nodes.client: Just go. Guys, let's get out of here.

ending.title: The group shuts you out
ending.text: Kuba and the group left. In street outreach one bad contact can close off access to the whole group for a long time.
